## Income Limits for Elderly and Disabled

For households with an elderly or disabled member, the gross monthly income limit is 130% of poverty level ($3,722 for a household of 8, with $492 to add for each additional person). However, for households which contain an elderly or disabled member, these income limits may not apply, and households with an elderly or disabled member must meet only the net income eligibility standards for SNAP unless categorically eligible.

## Who Qualifies

You may be able to get SNAP benefits if you are elderly or disabled and are low-income. Any household member who is age 60 or older or have a documented disability will meet an exemption from work requirements and may qualify for a medical deduction.

## Special Provisions for Elderly Households

South Carolina offers an Elderly Simplified Application Project (ESAP) to improve the SNAP process for elderly households. To qualify for ESAP, all household members must be elderly (age 60 or older), have no earned income, and the household's total monthly income must not exceed the income limit for the household size.

## Separate Household Status

An elderly person (60 years of age or older) who is unable to purchase and prepare meals due to a permanent disability may be considered, together with their spouse, a separate household from others. This separate household status must not be granted when the income of the others with whom the elderly disabled individual resides exceeds 165 percent of the poverty level.

content.content:
# SNAP Benefit Calculation Method

According to 7 CFR § 273.10(e)(2)(ii)(A), the household's monthly allotment is determined as follows:

"the household's monthly allotment shall be equal to the maximum SNAP allotment for the household's size reduced by 30 percent of the household's net monthly income"

The regulation provides two rounding options:

1. "round the 30 percent of net income up to the nearest higher dollar"

2. Alternatively, do not round the 30 percent figure. Instead, "after subtracting the 30 percent of net income from the appropriate Thrifty Food Plan, the State agency shall round the allotment down to the nearest lower dollar."

In summary, state agencies subtract one-third of the household's net monthly income from the maximum benefit amount for that household size, using one of the two specified rounding approaches.

I get $0 a year, the same as the reference. The answer turns on whether the head counts as "disabled" under SNAP's own definition, and the listed facts don't establish that.

2. **Disability status.** SNAP does not use a general "is disabled" flag. Under 7 U.S.C. 2012(j) and 7 CFR 271.2, a member counts as disabled only if they are 60 or older or receive a listed benefit. Those benefits include SSI, Social Security disability payments, permanent government disability retirement, VA total disability, Railroad Retirement disability, and disability-based Medicaid. The prompt lists only generic "disability benefits" and is silent on the source. It says not to infer unlisted benefit receipt, so I can't find that any listed benefit is received. The head is 53, so the household has no elderly or disabled member. As a side note, $2,139 a month in wages would be above the 2026 earnings limit for Social Security disability (about $1,690 a month, which I couldn't open on ssa.gov). That makes it unlikely the benefit is Social Security disability, but I don't rely on this.
3. **Gross income test.** Households without an elderly or disabled member must pass both the gross and net income tests (7 CFR 273.9(a)). The FY2026 gross limit for one person is $1,696 (130% of poverty). Secondary sources say South Carolina's broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE) removes the asset test but keeps that 130% income limit; I couldn't open the official SC DSS documents to confirm. $3,325.75 is above $1,696, so the household is not eligible.
